claims.text: Heat treatment can introduce a hierarchical microstructure in a high-entropy superalloy.
A heat-treatment-induced hierarchical microstructure can improve dynamic strength–ductility performance.
The initial material is a single-crystal high-entropy superalloy.
The initial material has an FCC structure.
The hierarchical structural mediator consists of nanosized disordered FCC particles inside ordered L12 precipitates.
Relevant tensile testing can be performed at temperatures up to 1023 K and at a strain rate of 10^-3 s^-1.
The nanosized disordered FCC particles act as obstacles to dislocation motion.
The nanosized disordered FCC particles pin superdislocations.
Pinning by the nanosized particles increases the energy required for dislocation motion.
The proposed dislocation-pinning mechanism enhances yield strength.
The heat-treated alloy will have improved high-temperature tensile yield strength relative to an untreated alloy without the hierarchical microstructure.
The heat-treated alloy will have improved high-temperature ductility relative to an untreated alloy without the hierarchical microstructure.
The predicted benefit should hold from 298 K to 1173 K at a strain rate of 10^-3 s^-1.
The long-term stability of the hierarchical microstructure and its effect on creep resistance are uncertain.

contradictions.description: The conditions specify high temperatures only up to 1023 K, whereas the boundary extends the claimed range to 1173 K.

The hypothesis targets dynamic performance, but the only specified strain rate is 10^-3 s^-1, which is a conventional quasi-static tensile-test rate rather than a dynamic or high-strain-rate condition.
